captions.text: Shortly before midnight, in a village called Nantes, somebody looked at a parked
locomotive and saw flames on the front of it.
They called 911.
The firefighters who arrived did exactly what they were trained to do, and they did
it correctly.
What nobody standing in that yard knew was that the engine they were about to switch
off was the only thing holding seventy-two tank cars of crude oil on the hill above
a sleeping town.
This is a story about a repair, a rule, a test, and a shift that ended.
Everything in it was signed off by somebody.
The repair was approved.
The train was secured, and a test was carried out to confirm it.
The operation had been approved by the country's transport regulator.
At the end of it, forty-seven people were dead, and eighteen separate things had
gone wrong.
Over the next half hour you will see how a parked train releases itself, what the
rule about that actually said, who was told and who was not told, and why the only
criminal trial that came out of it ended the way it did.
The question is not who to blame.
It is how a system can be arranged so that every step is somebody's job, and the
whole thing is nobody's.
In October of 2012, eight months before any of this, the locomotive that would end
up at the front of that train failed.
It went to the railway's own repair shop.
A diesel locomotive engine is not a car engine.
The block is a structure.
When something inside it breaks, the repair is heavy: the engine comes apart, the
damaged section is machined or replaced, and the locomotive sits out of service
while that happens.
That costs two things a railway does not like spending.
Time, and money.
There was also pressure to get the locomotive back into service.
So the engine was repaired with an epoxy-like material.
The investigation's own words for that material are worth hearing exactly.
It lacked the strength and the durability required for this use.
Inside that repair, a bearing was seated.
When the bolt holding it was tightened, it was tightened too far, and the bearing
cracked.
Nothing happened.
That is the part that matters.
The locomotive went back out and worked for eight months, and at no point in those
eight months did anyone looking at it have a reason to think it was carrying a
fracture.
A cam bearing is a small thing.
It supports the shaft that opens and closes the valves, and the whole of its job is
to sit still and let oil through.
A power assembly is one cylinder's worth of engine — piston, liner, head, valves —
and a locomotive of this kind has a row of them.
What a cracked cam bearing does is quiet and slow.
It reduces the oil reaching the valves at the top of one power assembly.
Less oil means more heat and more wear.
The valves were damaged.
Eventually a piston crown was punctured.
A punctured piston lets oil past, and the oil went where the exhaust goes, which is
into the turbocharger.
A turbocharger is driven by exhaust gas and it runs hot enough to glow.
So oil collected in a hot metal casing for eight months.
On the afternoon of the fifth of July, twenty thirteen, that locomotive left the
yard at Farnham, Quebec, at about five to two.
It was going to Nantes, where the crew would change, and then on to Saint John, New
Brunswick.
Behind it were seventy-two loaded tank cars, a buffer car, four more locomotives and
a remote-control car.
The whole thing weighed about ten thousand two hundred and ninety tons.
The cargo was petroleum crude oil, loaded at New Town, in North Dakota.
Seven point seven million litres of it.
One person was operating it.
A single locomotive engineer, in the lead locomotive, under the railway's
single-person operating instructions.
The run was about a hundred and eighteen miles and it took roughly nine hours.
And the man who cleared that train to leave Farnham told the court, four years
later, that he had given the go-ahead without knowing the lead locomotive was
defective.
The cars themselves were a type called Class 111.
They were the ordinary tank car of North American railways at the time, and by the
end of this story they would not be.
At ten minutes to eleven that night, the train stopped at Nantes.
Nantes was the designated crew change point.
A train arrives, one crew stops work, another takes it on.
That arrangement exists because there are limits on how long a person may work a
train, and because a run of this length crosses more than one of them.
The train does not stop for the night.
The people do.
So a train standing at a crew change point is a normal thing.
It is standing there waiting for the next person.
What was not routine, and what the investigation would spend a great deal of its
length on, is where the train was standing when it stopped.
It was parked on a descending grade, on the main track.
Just over seven miles away, at the bottom of that grade, was the town of
Lac-Mégantic.
A parked train is held by two different things, and the difference between them is
the whole of this film.
The first is the air brake.
Air brakes are held on by pressure.
That pressure is made by a compressor, and the compressor is driven by a running
locomotive engine.
The second is the hand brake.
A hand brake is a wheel on the end of a car that a person turns, by hand, one car at
a time, in the dark.
It does not need pressure.
It does not need anything.
Once it is on, it stays on.
Here is the sequence that night, as the recorders and the investigation put it back
together.
There are two air brakes on a train like this, and they are not the same thing.
The automatic brake works the whole train, every car, through a pipe that runs from
one end to the other.
The independent brake works only the locomotives at the front.
Both of them need air.
Both of them need something to be making that air.
The train was stopped using the automatic brakes.
The independent brakes were applied.
The automatic brakes were then released.
Four of the trailing locomotives were shut down.
So from that moment the seventy-two loaded cars behind the locomotives had no air
brake holding them at all.
What was holding them was whatever the locomotives at the front could hold, and
seven hand brakes.
And hand brakes were applied to seven.
Seven, out of a train of seventy-eight vehicles.
And all seven were on the locomotives and the buffer car.
Not one hand brake was applied to any of the seventy-two tank cars.
It is worth picturing what applying them actually involves, because it is not a
switch.
A person walks the length of the train in the dark, climbs up at each car, and turns
a wheel until the chain is tight.
On a train of seventy-two loaded cars, walking one end to the other is most of a
mile, and every one of those wheels has to be turned by the same pair of arms.
That is the shape of the decision.
Not a rule ignored, but a task whose cost falls entirely on one person at the end of
a shift, in the dark, with nothing telling him it is not already enough.
Now, the railway had a rule about this, and it was not a vague one.
Its own instructions set a minimum by a formula: ten per cent of the cars, plus two.
For this train that is seventy-two divided by ten, plus two.
Nine point two.
Nine.
Seven were applied.
The railway's own minimum, by the railway's own arithmetic, was nine.
And the investigation, working out what it would actually have taken to hold ten
thousand tons on that grade with no air, concluded that the real number was a
minimum of seventeen, and possibly as many as twenty-six.
But none of that was left to judgement, because there was a test.
The rules required the crew to release all the air brakes and then let the slack in
the train adjust itself — by gravity, or by trying to move the train slightly with
the locomotive.
And the standard the rule set is one sentence long.
It must be apparent, when the slack runs in or out, that the hand brakes are
sufficient to prevent that cut of cars from moving.
That is a good rule.
If you do that and the train stays where it is, the hand brakes are enough.
If it moves, they are not, and you go and set more.
The test was performed.
It was performed with the independent brakes still active.
The air was not fully released.
So the thing holding the train during the test was not the thing being tested.
The train held.
Of course it held.
And because it held, nobody in that yard had any way of knowing that seven hand
brakes were not enough.
It is worth being precise here, because this is the point where the story is usually
told wrongly.
This was not a man skipping a check.
The check was done.
It was the check itself that could not fail.
At three minutes past eleven, the automatic brakes were released.
The recorder on the locomotive logged the time to the second.
From that moment the train was held by the independent brakes on the locomotives,
which needed the compressor, which needed an engine to be running — and by seven
hand brakes, which did not.
The paperwork was correct.
The rule had been complied with as the crew understood it.
And the train was standing on a hill held largely by something that would not still
be there in two hours.
By the accounts published afterwards, the engineer finished his shift and went to a
hotel in the town at the bottom of the hill.
At about half past eleven, a taxi driver arrived at the yard to collect the
engineer, and noticed heavy smoke and droplets of oil coming off the locomotive.
He told the court, four years later, that clouds of black smoke were billowing from
the stack.
Shortly before midnight, the fire was reported to 911, and the Nantes fire
department responded.
The provincial police told the rail traffic controller, seventy miles away in
Farnham, that a train of his was on fire.
The railway tried to send someone who understood locomotives.
It could not reach anyone with locomotive engineering experience, so it sent a track
foreman — a man whose job is the rails, not the engines.
Consider what that means for the next hour.
The person the railway put at the scene was qualified to tell you about the ground
the train was standing on.
He was not the person you would send to answer the question that mattered, which was
what happens to the brakes on this train if the engine that was on fire stays off.
And that question was never formally put.
The railway's controller was seventy miles away, working from what he was told.
The fire service's job was the fire, and the fire was out.
The fire service did the correct thing for a fire on a diesel engine.
You cut the fuel and you cut the power.
They used the emergency fuel shut-off switch.
They moved the electrical breakers inside the cab to the off position.
The fire went out.
Nobody was hurt at Nantes.
The firefighters and the track foreman then left, after discussions with the rail
traffic controller in Farnham.
One of the volunteers went home in the small hours, having helped put out a fire on
a locomotive that had been supplying the power for the air brakes.
And here is the sentence in the report that does the most work of any sentence in
it.
No decision was documented, after the fire was extinguished, to move the train or to
apply additional hand brakes.
Not a refusal.
Not an argument.
No decision.
With every locomotive shut down, the air compressor stopped supplying the air brake
system.
Air brakes do not fail suddenly.
They leak.
The pressure holding a ten-thousand-ton train on a descending grade fell, slowly, in
an empty yard, with nobody watching it, for about an hour and a half.
Nothing was happening in that hour and a half.
That is the accurate description of it.
The fire was out.
The crews had gone.
The yard was dark.
A train was standing where it had been left, and the number on a gauge nobody was
looking at was going down.
At fifty-eight minutes past midnight and twenty-one seconds, the train began to
move.
One mile an hour.
A ten-thousand-ton train at one mile an hour is a thing a person could walk beside.
There was no person.
The pressure in the brake pipe at the back of the train, measured at that moment,
was twenty-nine pounds per square inch.
There was nobody on it.
Seven point two miles of descending grade, no driver, no brake that was coming back,
and a town at the bottom.
Seventeen minutes later it was doing sixty-five miles an hour.
The track into Lac-Mégantic does not run straight.
At mile zero point two three there is a curve — four and a quarter degrees,
right-handed, banked by about an inch.
The speed that curve is built for is eighteen to twenty-two miles an hour.
The train entered it at sixty-five.
The investigation's finding on that is exact.
A combination of the centrifugal force and the dynamic forces generated by the track
geometry, at a speed of sixty-five miles an hour, was sufficient to cause the
derailment.
The derailment itself lasted about one minute.
Sixty-three of the seventy-two tank cars came off the track.
The locomotives broke away, split into two groups, and carried on for four thousand
four hundred feet.
Then the leading group rolled back down the grade, four hundred and seventy-five
feet, struck the group behind it, and the two of them moved another hundred feet
before anything stopped.
Approximately six million litres of crude oil were released.
In the hours after it, firefighters went street by street through the houses nearest
the derailment and moved about a thousand people out to build a perimeter.
By the time the evacuation was complete, about two thousand people had left their
homes.
That is roughly a third of the town.
Fire crews came from across the surrounding region, and it took until the following
afternoon to bring the fire under control.
Forty homes and businesses were destroyed, and the power was out for a long time
afterwards.
In the weeks that followed, the response drew in the town's own leadership, fire
services, criminal investigators, coroners, environmental staff, and health and
social services, coordinated by the province's civil protection ministry.
Forty-seven people were killed.
Much of the centre of the town was destroyed.
By the accounts published afterwards, more than thirty buildings in the town centre
were lost, and most of what was left had to be taken down because the ground was
contaminated.
Before the investigation reached any question of who did what, it looked at the tank
cars, and what it found there is its own kind of answer.
All sixty-three of the derailed cars had been built to a single specification,
between nineteen eighty and twenty twelve.
Seventy-eight per cent of them were less than five years old.
None of them had thermal protection, and the regulations did not require it on cars
of that class.
Fifty-nine of the sixty-three were breached.
Ninety-four per cent.
Thirty-seven of them were holed through the shell.
Thirty-one were punctured through the head, which is the flat end of the barrel.
Twenty had their fittings torn off.
And the finding on those cars reads like this.
All sixty-three derailed tank cars were in compliance with the specification
requirement that was in effect at the time of their approval and construction.
They were legal.
They were current.
Ninety-four per cent of them opened.
That sentence is the one to keep.
Compliance is not a description of how strong something is.
It is a description of what was asked of it, on the day it was approved.
A car built in nineteen eighty and a car built in twenty twelve were both in
compliance, because the requirement had not moved between them.
Seventy-eight per cent of the cars that came off the track that night were less than
five years old.
The Transportation Safety Board investigated for just over a year, and in August of
twenty fourteen it published what it had found.
It identified eighteen distinct causes and contributing factors.
This film is not going to read all eighteen out.
A list of eighteen is a thing you stop hearing at about number five, and the point
of them is not the items.
The point is the shape they make.
Eighteen is a strange number to be handed at the end of a story like this, because
it is not an answer.
It is the refusal of one.
Some of the eighteen were about that night.
Most were not.
The railway had a safety management system.
It had written one in two thousand and two.
It did not begin implementing it until two thousand and ten.
And by twenty thirteen it was still not functioning effectively.
That is eleven years in which a document existed and the thing it described did not.
The regulator's regional office did not audit that system until twenty ten.
And the rule about hand brakes — the ten per cent plus two, the rule that produced
the number nine — was the railway's own.
Transport Canada does not validate a railway company's special instructions, and it
gives no specific guidance on how many hand brakes must be applied to a parked
freight train.
And the cargo was not what its papers said.
The crude oil in those cars was more volatile than the shipping documents described.
That matters, because volatility is what decides whether a derailment is a spill or
a fire.
Dangerous goods are sorted into packing groups, and the group is what tells
everybody down the line how careful to be.
Group one is the most dangerous.
Group three is the least.
This crude was shipped as packing group three.
The least dangerous option available for crude oil.
It should have been group two.
The Board found that its vapour pressure was high and its flashpoint was low, which
in plain terms means it was readily ignitable.
The oil was loaded and papered by a company in Minnesota.
Afterwards, the federal transport minister ordered companies to test crude before
shipping it, so that what was written on the papers matched what was in the car.
The Board called for physical defences against runaway trains, and for more thorough
audits of safety management systems.
Its formal recommendations went further than that, and they are worth reading as a
set, because together they describe a system rather than a night.
The first was about the cars.
It asked Canada and the United States to require that every Class 111 tank car
carrying flammable liquids meet an enhanced protection standard — one that
significantly reduces the risk of losing the product in an accident.
The Board's reason for that is one line, and it is the line that answers the
ninety-four per cent.
The damage clearly indicated that product release could have been reduced had the
tank car shells and heads been more impact-resistant.
The second was about the running of the trains.
It asked for stringent criteria for operating a train that carries dangerous goods,
and it asked that railways be required to plan and analyse their routes, and to
carry out periodic risk assessments to confirm that their own controls actually
work.
That last clause is the whole film in eleven words.
To confirm that their own controls actually work.
And the third asked Transport Canada to require additional physical defences against
runaway equipment.
Not a rule.
Not a form.
Something on the ground that stops a train that has started to move.
And there is one sentence the report did not write, which is the sentence almost
everybody expects.
The train was operated that night by one person.
It has been argued ever since that a second crew member would have changed what
happened.
The investigation was not able to conclude that.
Single-person operation is not among the eighteen.
What the regulator did is a separate fact, and it happened quickly.
Seventeen days after the derailment, Transport Canada issued an emergency directive.
It required at least two people to operate a train carrying tank cars of dangerous
goods.
It prohibited leaving such a train unattended on a main track.
It required the cabs of unattended trains to be locked and the reverser handles
removed, so the train could not be put into gear.
It set hand-brake requirements for any train left unattended for more than an hour,
and for anything left an hour or less it required both the automatic brake and the
independent brake to be applied at their maximum.
Those directives took effect immediately and ran to December.
In July of twenty fifteen the whole of it was written into Rule 112 of the Canadian
Railway Operating Rules, permanently, and in more detail.
Every one of those requirements describes something that was not required on the
fifth of July, twenty thirteen.
The United States moved too.
On the second of August, its rail regulator issued an emergency order of its own,
about the attendance and securing of freight trains left standing outside a yard.
Quebec, for its part, ordered the railway to pay for the cleanup.
In August of twenty thirteen, the railway and its Canadian subsidiary filed for
bankruptcy protection.
It did not have enough insurance to cover the claims against it.
Its assets were sold in January of twenty fourteen, and the line went on operating
under a new name.
A settlement fund was assembled for the victims, and in October of twenty fifteen a
United States bankruptcy judge approved it.
It came to somewhere between four hundred and forty-six and four hundred and fifty
million Canadian dollars, and about twenty-five companies paid into it.
A settlement fund is not a verdict.
Nobody who pays into one is found to have done anything.
It is an amount of money agreed by companies who would otherwise be in court for
years, and it is how almost every disaster of this size is actually resolved.
Twenty-five of them agreed to that.
One did not.
Canadian Pacific was the only company accused in the disaster that refused to
contribute.
It maintained that it bore no responsibility, and it asked for permission to appeal
the settlement's approval.
It later dropped its objection, and the fund was approved.
And then there was a criminal trial.
It opened in Sherbrooke in October of twenty seventeen, before a bilingual jury.
Three men were charged with criminal negligence causing forty-seven deaths.
The locomotive engineer, fifty-six.
The rail traffic controller, fifty-nine.
The manager of train operations, fifty-three.
They were the three people at the operating end of everything this film has
described.
The Crown's case was that a train weighing more than ten thousand tonnes had not
been properly secured, that it had been left on a slope ten kilometres from the
town, and that the explosion could have been avoided if the workers had done their
jobs properly.
The defence called no witnesses.
And there is one thing about that trial which has to be said carefully, because it
is not a criticism of the jury.
Before the trial began, the judge ruled the Transportation Safety Board's report
inadmissible.
The jury did not consider any of the Board's conclusions.
The eighteen findings this film has spent the last twenty minutes on were not
evidence in the only criminal trial that arose from them.
The jury did hear some of it from other directions.
It heard expert evidence that the only other railway in Quebec running one-person
crews had to satisfy sixty-nine conditions imposed by the regulator before it could
adopt them, and that this railway had to comply with one.
One condition.
A mirror on the driver's side of the lead locomotive.
One-person crews had been brought in on that run months before the disaster.
They were discontinued the day after it.
The engineer's lawyer wanted to argue to the jury that one-man crews were not safe.
That argument was made in the jury's absence, and the judge rejected it.
And it is worth knowing what the jury was actually being asked, because it is not
the question most people assume.
The judge instructed them that to convict, the accused must have failed to do
something they were required to do, in a way that showed a reckless disregard for
the lives of others, and that this must have caused the deaths of the forty-seven.
And the standard he set for that was a marked and substantial departure from what a
reasonable person would do.
Not a mistake.
Not even a serious mistake.
A marked and substantial departure — and the burden of showing it rested entirely on
the Crown.
He also told them to decide it without regard to public opinion, in a case where an
entire country had one.
They asked more than once for the instructions to be explained again.
At one point they reached an impasse, and were asked to keep going.
In January of twenty eighteen, after nine days of deliberation, the jury acquitted
all three.
The engineer said afterwards that he was deeply sorry.
That is not the end of the legal record, and the rest of it matters just as much.
The month after the acquittal, the railway itself pleaded guilty to a federal
offence and was fined a million dollars.
Six former employees pleaded guilty to breaking the Railway Safety Act —
specifically, to failing to test the hand brakes after they had been applied.
Five of them were fined fifty thousand dollars each.
The six included the company's chief executive, its general manager of
transportation, its director of operating practices, its assistant director of
operations, its operations manager, and the engineer.
The engineer received a conditional sentence of six months, served in the community.
So the record holds both of these things at once.
Three men were acquitted of criminal negligence causing death.
And six men, from the chief executive down to the engineer, admitted a regulatory
offence about the test.
The rules did change.
Canada ordered the tank car in this story out of crude oil service by November of
twenty sixteen, six months earlier than had originally been planned.
A stronger design replaced it, and from April of twenty twenty-five it became the
only tank car allowed to carry flammable liquids in the country.
The cleaning up was its own decade.
Decontaminating the ground was estimated at about a hundred and fifty million
dollars, and cleaning the river that runs out of the lake at about fifty million
more.
The federal government agreed to cover half of the decontamination, to a maximum of
ninety-five million.
The mayor said at the time that the town expected the work to take about eighteen
months.
The old main street was called Frontenac.
It had shops on it, and restaurants, a dentist's office, a grocery store.
All of it was destroyed, and the town built a new main street a few hundred metres
away.
What they built in its place was not a copy of what was lost.
The streets were laid on an axis with the lake so the air moves through them.
There are wider bike paths with trees along them.
Twenty-two hundred solar panels went onto the roofs downtown, wired into a local
grid that serves about thirty buildings.
Ten years on, residents were saying the downtown still had not really come back.
And ten years on, freight trains were still running through the middle of the town.
There is a plan for that.
A new rail corridor, twelve and a half kilometres long, around the town instead of
through it.
It was costed in twenty eighteen at a hundred and thirty-three million dollars,
sixty per cent federal and forty per cent provincial.
In December of twenty twenty-two both governments agreed to put more money in, at
the same split.
The federal government took possession of the land it needed in August of twenty
twenty-three, by expropriation.
The contribution agreement with the province was signed in July of twenty
twenty-four.
When it is finished, the line through the town is to be taken up, so that the centre
can finally be rebuilt.
The bypass has to run somewhere, and where it runs is through the municipalities
next door.
In January of twenty twenty-three, Nantes — the village where the train was parked —
withdrew its support for the project.
The month after that, a referendum in the neighbouring municipality of Frontenac
showed a majority of residents against it.
So here is what the record holds.
A repair made with the wrong material because the right one cost time and money.
Seven hand brakes where the railway's own rule said nine and the physics said at
least seventeen.
A test that could not have failed.
An hour and a half in which no decision was documented.
Tank cars that were fully compliant and opened anyway.
A safety system that existed on paper for eleven years.
A regulator that audited it once, three years before.
Eighteen findings.
A company that no longer exists.
Three men acquitted of criminal negligence, and six who admitted a regulatory
offence about a test.
And a jury that was never permitted to see the findings at all.
No individual was ever established as the cause of it.
And there are things this film cannot tell you, because they are not in what has
been published.
What the night cost any one person who lived through it is not in the record we have
read.
That is not a loose end.
That is the finding.
Every system you depend on is arranged the same way.
Somebody approves the repair.
Somebody writes the rule.
Somebody performs the test.
Somebody signs the audit, or does not.
Each of those people is doing a job that is defined, and bounded, and complete on
its own terms.
The question is never whether one of them fails.
It is whether anybody in the whole arrangement is responsible for the arrangement.
In this case the answer, tested in a criminal court over four months and nine days
of deliberation, was that no one could be shown to have departed markedly and
substantially from what a reasonable person would do.
Which may be exactly right, and is also the reason a report with eighteen findings
exists at all.
The findings are what is left when the question of blame has been asked properly and
has come back empty.
Seventeen days after the town burned, the rules changed.
It took a runaway train, a destroyed downtown and forty-seven deaths for a
requirement to exist that a train carrying this cargo may not be left alone on a
main track.

Eight months before the accident, the lead locomotive goes to the repair shop after an engine failure. (LM-20)
Given the time and cost of a standard repair, and the pressure to return the locomotive to service, the engine is repaired with an epoxy-like polymeric material. (LM-21)
Its mounting bolt is over-tightened during that repair. The bearing fractures, oil to the valve train falls away, and oil begins accumulating where it should not. (LM-22, LM-23)
72 Class 111 tank cars of petroleum crude, loaded at New Town, North Dakota. 7.7 million litres. (LM-01, LM-02)

MMA developed one in 2002, did not begin implementing it until 2010, and by 2013 it was still not functioning effectively. (LM-26)
Transport Canada's Quebec office did not audit that system until 2010, and does not validate a railway's special instructions or say how many hand brakes a train needs. (LM-27, LM-30)

The crude was classified Packing Group III - the least dangerous option - when it should have been Packing Group II. High vapour pressure and low flashpoint made it readily ignitable. (LM-102, LM-103)
All 63 derailed cars met the specification in force when they were built. None had thermal protection, and the regulations did not require it. (LM-64, LM-65)

Sherbrooke, October 2017 to January 2018, before a bilingual jury. (LM-69, LM-71)
The jury asked for its instructions to be clarified more than once, and reached an impasse, before returning the verdict in January 2018. (LM-35, LM-108)

Separately, six former MMA employees pleaded guilty under the Railway Safety Act, among them the chief executive. The engineer received a six-month conditional sentence served in the community. (LM-77, LM-78, LM-79)
MMA entered bankruptcy protection in August 2013 with insufficient insurance. A US judge approved a settlement fund of about C$446 million; some 25 companies contributed. (LM-31, LM-33)
Transport Canada issued an emergency directive requiring at least two people to operate a train carrying dangerous goods. Formalised in Rule 112 in July 2015. (LM-89, LM-91)
